This metabolic value, obtained from adult individuals resting within their thermoneutral zone, underscores the energetic demands of a medium-bodied nocturnal primate. Field records indicate that adult females of this species typically attain an ultimate body mass of approximately 734 grams [Wwi = approximately 734 grams], although considerable sexual dimorphism exists; males are substantially larger, with some individuals reaching up to 1314 grams [Wwi = up to 1314 grams]. The considerable variation in adult body mass, ranging from about half a kilogram to over a kilogram, likely reflects differences in local resource availability and individual condition across the species' range in coastal East Africa. These mass data, derived from both wild-caught specimens and captive colony records, provide a necessary foundation for interpreting the species' metabolic scaling and its life-history trade-offs.

Reproductive output in Northern greater galago is constrained by a relatively slow life-history pace characteristic of many strepsirrhines. Females typically produce a single offspring per year [Ri = single offspring per year] and the maximum reproduction rate corresponds to one litter per year under the thermal conditions typical of their active metabolic regime at 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. Neonates weigh just 46 grams [Wwb = 46 grams] at birth, a birth mass that is relatively modest compared to the adult female mass, reflecting the altricial state of the newborn. This extended gestation period, followed by a long period of dependency, shapes the species' overall reproductive strategy.

The developmental trajectory from birth to nutritional independence in Otolemur garnettii follows a protracted schedule. Weaning, defined as the cessation of milk ingestion and the completion of the transition to solid foods, occurs at approximately 140 days after birth [tx = approximately 140 days after birth], maintained under standard colony temperatures of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. At this critical juncture, the weaned offspring have attained a wet weight of 467 grams [Wwx = 467 grams], representing roughly one-third of the typical adult female mass. The length of the suckling period, spanning several months, allows for substantial growth and the development of essential locomotor and foraging skills necessary for independent survival in the complex three-dimensional environment of the coastal forest. The steady mass gain from the neonatal stage to weaning reflects a period of intensive maternal investment through milk production.

Sexual maturation in this species is a relatively late phenomenon, consistent with its position along the slow end of the primate life-history continuum. Puberty, marked by the attainment of full reproductive capacity and behavioral independence from the mother, is reached at 600 days after birth [tp = 600 days after birth], a developmental milestone recorded under captive rearing conditions at 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This extended juvenile period, lasting nearly two years, is hypothesized to be necessary for young galagos to acquire the complex foraging knowledge and social competencies required for successful territory establishment and mate acquisition. During this prolonged pre-reproductive phase, individuals continue to grow, gradually approaching their adult body mass, and must navigate the challenges of predator avoidance and food competition within their natal home range. The delay in reproductive maturity represents a significant investment in somatic growth and learning at the expense of early breeding opportunities.

Longevity data from both captive colonies and field studies indicate that the maximum lifespan of Otolemur garnettii is approximately 3650 days [am = approximately 3650 days], recorded in individuals maintained at a stable body temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This lifespan, while modest by primate standards, is relatively long for a mammal of its body size and aligns with the species' overall slow life-history syndrome characterized by low reproductive output and extended developmental periods. The substantial growth trajectory from a modest birth mass of 46 grams [Wwb = 46 grams] to an eventual adult mass in males of over 1314 grams [Wwi = over 1314 grams] highlights the considerable energetic investment required throughout this long life. Senescence in older individuals has been observed in captive settings, with geriatric animals showing reduced activity levels and diminished sensory acuity before natural death.
